blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Name the macroeconomic aims of government, state the indicator behind each, and explain whom each aim serves.

blocks.heading: The five aims
blocks.text: The macroeconomic aims of government are the economy-wide outcomes a government works towards: low inflation, low unemployment, steady growth in the output of the economy, a current account close to balance, and redistribution of income towards a fairer distribution. They are macroeconomic because each describes the whole economy rather than one market: the general price level, not the price of one bag of maize meal; the share of the workforce without jobs across the country, not the staff of one shop in Katutura; the spread of incomes across all households, not the pay of one family. A ministry in Windhoek and a ministry in Tokyo list the same five aims, because they describe conditions an economy can be in rather than policies one government favours. The aims are destinations; the policy tools that pursue them come in topics 4.3 to 4.5.

blocks.heading: Reading the aims in figures
blocks.text: Each aim is read off an indicator. Low inflation is measured by the rate of inflation, the percentage rise in the general price level over a year. The jobs aim is measured by the unemployment rate, the percentage of the labour force without work but seeking it. Growth is measured by the annual percentage rise in real output of the whole economy, external balance is read from the current account balance, and progress towards a fairer distribution of income is read from whether the gap between high and low household incomes narrows. So a learner in Walvis Bay reading that inflation slowed to 4.1%, unemployment stood at 12.6%, output grew by 3.0% and the current account deficit reached 3.4% of export value can say which aims the economy moved towards and which it missed.

blocks.heading: Whom each aim serves
blocks.text: Low inflation tends to protect the buying power of wages and savings, so a worker in Gobabis whose pay rises by 5.0% while prices rise by 3.0% is better off in real terms, and savers and people on fixed pensions hold their ground when price rises stay slow. Low unemployment raises household incomes, keeps skills from fading and lifts tax revenue while cutting support payments. Steady growth raises the output and average incomes the economy can sustain, where the gains are shared out across households. A current account close to balance means a country is not persistently spending more abroad than it earns, which steadies its repayments to foreign lenders. A fairer distribution of income narrows the gap between rich and poor households, so more families can afford basics such as food, schooling and clinic visits. The importance of each aim varies with circumstances: where unemployment is high, jobs tend to lead the ranking; where prices are rising fast, inflation tends to lead.

blocks.text: The aims assume the role of government set out in topic 4.1; growth is measured in topic 4.6 and unemployment in topic 4.7.
